name: Adam Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is kept confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Karin and I farm Elmstead, 350 hectares that my grandfather started with 40. We grow potatoes, sugar beet and wheat, and finish 200 beef cattle a year on the beet tops and grass. Our son Erik, who's 30, works with me full time, and we've two staff. I start at six on my phone, asking the AI assistant for the spray window and the potato store temperatures, then it's out with Erik.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love trying new things that pay, like the GPS steering on the tractors, which cut our fuel and seed bills by about 8%. I'm the one at the farm show asking the salesman awkward questions. What wears me out is the government changing the rules every two years, and the supermarket potato contract, which gets tighter every season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, because I was looking forward to it. At the machinery ring I'd say keep using the tools that pay and ignore the rest. Online I'd post the numbers from our GPS steering, because numbers beat opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I already get my money's worth out of the AI assistant and the GPS. The potato contract and the government's rule changes were always bigger risks to Elmstead than a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the AI for planning and records and try the new variable-rate fertiliser spreader, about 18,000. I'd keep our five months of savings and not borrow more. I'd keep training Erik to run the business side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit disappointed. I like progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the supermarket squeezed the potato contract further?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sell more potatoes through the local wholesaler and grow less for the supermarket. Erik's been pushing for a farm shop too. I'd rather make money from my own customers than beg a buyer for a penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Karin see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karin runs the office and the holiday cottage, and she thinks I spend too much on gadgets. She's usually right about the ones that don't pay. We have a rule: nothing over 10,000 without both of us agreeing.

Keep the tools that **pay** and ignore the rest.
I'd post our **GPS numbers**, because numbers beat opinions.
think: I'd be **fine**, already getting value from AI and GPS.
The **potato contract** and rule changes are the bigger risks.
do: Keep **five months** of savings and borrow no more.
Keep training **Erik** on the business side.

fieldNote: He's an **eager adopter** who'd actually miss the change.

Sell more potatoes through the local wholesaler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farmers who are willing to learn. At the machinery ring I'd offer to show people how I use it. Online I'd say the government should get out of the way and let farms adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Elmstead comes out ahead. Most of what AI takes on a farm is the office work, and that frees me and Karin to do more selling. The farms that struggle will be the ones that wait for the government to tell them what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd put all our records, planning and ordering on AI, and give Karin her evenings back. I'd buy a share in a robot weeder with two neighbours through the machinery ring, maybe 25,000 each. I'd send Erik on a precision farming course in the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two staff, Piotr and Dave, are hands-on and good, so they're safe for now. The ones I'd worry about are the agronomists and sales reps who sell us advice. AI will do a lot of their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should get out of the way. Is there anything you'd want from it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer forms and stable rules, that's all. And maybe apprenticeships, so young people learn the machines on real farms, not in classrooms. I'd take an apprentice tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers who move fast will do well, and the rest need to move now. At the machinery ring I'd suggest we buy robots together. Online I'd say this isn't the time for more rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side by 2028 I'm ready for. The worry is 2031, when everybody gets the robots at once and potato and beef prices drop. Robots make every farm cheaper to run, so the supermarkets will just pay less for potatoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd talk to the bank about a loan for robot potato harvesting, but only if the machinery ring shares the cost. I'd sign a three-year contract with the wholesaler now, before prices fall. I'd also help Piotr and Dave train as robot technicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but two years is quick even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three years between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're the years to get organised. The planning and selling are already AI from 2028, so we spend those years choosing robots and lining up buyers. By 2031 I want to be ready, not reacting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Erik and the farm's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik would be the one running the robots, and he's keen. I'd hand him more of the business by 2030. My worry is whether the farm makes enough to pay two families once prices drop.

This isn't the time for **more rules**.

Supermarkets would simply **pay less** for potatoes.

fieldNote: He worries about **falling prices**, not his own job.
He looks after his **staff** by retraining them for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so plan. At the machinery ring I'd say let's agree a shared robot plan by 2032. Online I'd say no subsidies, just clear rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one suits me and Erik. I'm 63 when the thinking AI arrives and 66 for the robots, which is when I'd hand over anyway. With five years warning, my son Erik takes over Elmstead with the robots already working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a robot trial on one field of potatoes in 2029, shared through the machinery ring. I'd give Erik the cattle side to run from 2028. And I'd build our savings to six months and pay off the machinery loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan coming together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, always. If the supermarkets use robots to squeeze us early, we'd be paying for machines on lower income. That's why I'd rather share the robots than buy them alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Karin feel about the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karin would want to see the numbers first. I'd show her the trial results before we buy anything more. That's our deal.

say: The ring should agree a **shared robot plan** by 2032.
think: Robots at 66 match when I'd **hand over** anyway.
Erik takes over **with robots** already working.
do: Run a **robot trial** on one potato field in 2029.
Build savings to **six months** and pay off machinery loans.
S3.quote: With five years warning, my son Erik takes over Elmstead with the robots already working.
fieldNote: Five years lines up the robots with his **handover to Erik**.
He still names **price pressure** as the main risk.
He keeps the **household rule** with Karin on big spending.

steps.text: Run a shared robot trial on one potato field in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good runway and nobody should complain. At the machinery ring I'd say this is our chance to plan properly. Online I'd say leave it to farmers, not politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm relaxed. I'll have handed over to Erik before the robots arrive in 2039. Ten years is long enough to teach Erik (his son) everything and let the robots learn the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, try new tools as they come and keep the business growing. I'd hand Elmstead to Erik by 2032 and stay on as an adviser. Karin and I would put more into a pension and maybe buy the cottage outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sorry I'll miss the best part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably bother Erik with advice he doesn't want. And maybe teach apprentices at the machinery ring. I'd like young people to see that farming can be modern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The early mornings, no. The harvests, yes. There's nothing like a full potato store in October.

fieldNote: With a decade, he's **fully secure** and focused on succession.
He wants to **teach apprentices**, matching his traditional values.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots come before Erik's ready and before prices settle. What would help is stable rules for ten years, so we can plan, and apprenticeships so young people learn robots on real farms. Not handouts, just a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about families. A farm is a family business, and the best robot in the world won't take over from my son Erik. Somebody still has to love the place.

headlineQuote: A farm is a family business, and the best robot in the world won't take over from my son Erik.
portrait: Adam, 58, farms **350 hectares** of potatoes, beet, wheat and beef with his son Erik.
He uses **AI every day** and loves new tools that pay for themselves.
His standing pressures are **supermarket contracts** and changing government rules.
Even in the fast scenario he plans to **share robots** with neighbours and retrain his staff.
Free-market and family-minded, he aims to **hand the farm** to Erik with robots working.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots and lower prices arrive before Erik is ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Stable rules** for ten years so farms can plan.
**Apprenticeships** for young people to learn robots on real farms.
